newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Foreigners snap up S.Korean blue chips on new limit.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners snap up S.Korean blue chips on new limit.

text.p: Foreign investors snapped up South Korean blue chip shares on Friday, the first day of the increased ceiling on foreign-owned stocks, as domestic institutions fed their demand, brokers said.
The ceiling, which was increased to 23 percent from 20 percent, is applied to foreign holdings in individual companies.
Brokers said a familiar pattern had emerged in early Friday trading with domestic institutional investors selling into heavy foreign buying.
"It's a typical pattern that local institutions sell and foreigners try to accumulate their favourites on the first day of the ceiling expansion," said Park Key-pyong of Hanyang Securities.
An estimated 500 billion to one trillion won ($560 million to $1.12 billion) was expected to flow into South Korean stocks as a result of the new ceiling. The ceiling was last raised in October.
Shortly after trading opened on Friday, newly available shares of 27 stocks had already been sold out to foreigners, according to an official at the Korea Stock Exchange.
Among the sell-outs were expected favourites such as Samsung Electronics, POSCO and SK Telecom
But heavy institutional selling pushed down their prices. SK Telecom lost 21,000 won, or 4.8 percent, to 43,500 and POSCO shed 100 won to 53,500 by mid-morning.
Also selling out were Sungmi Telecom and Sam-A Aluminium, which are not considered blue chips.
Brokers said foreign investors bought Sungmi because of a strong interest in telecommunications shares, but said they could not explain the interest in Sam-A.
Brokers said the market would be mixed throughout Friday as the early morning trading pattern of domestic institutional selling into foreign buying was expected to be repeated.
"Many investors are closely watching movements by domestic institutional investors, who are becoming cash-rich after selling their holdings to foreigners," Park said.
He forecast institutions were likely to shift to recent laggards, including cheap large-capitalised shares.
Brokers said April's improved trade deficit had helped soothe investor sentiment. April's trade shortfall narrowed to $1.5 billion from $2.04 billion a year earlier.

They said financial troubles in the Ssangyong Group, which earlier announced a restructuring plan aimed at rescuing its automaking unit, and Jinro Group, which narrowly averted bankruptcy, would dent the market as investors were shying away from their shares.
Some brokers had predicted that foreign investors would buy only blue chips because of concerns about the corporate failures and South Korea's economic fundamentals.
